title: Turn a stakeholder interview into requirements
scenario:
Bazaarly wants more sellers live on the marketplace before the festive season. Onboarding has become slow and sellers complain. You interviewed Pooja for 30 minutes. Your notes:

> "Sellers start on web or app, upload PAN, GSTIN certificate, a cancelled cheque and an address proof. Then my KYC team checks everything by hand: four people, about 120 applications a day in peak. Since April we're at 8–9 days just for KYC; it used to be 4–5. Honestly a third of rejections are blurry photos; the seller only finds out a week later by email, re-uploads, and waits again. Bank name mismatches are next: the name on the cheque doesn't match the PAN. GSTIN we type into the GST portal one by one. Sellers keep calling to ask for status; we get maybe 200 calls a week. Field agents onboard some sellers in tier-2 towns and those go much smoother. Whatever we build has to work on low-end Android phones and 3G. Legal says we must keep KYC documents for 8 years and only my team can see them. Our target from leadership is 10 days from application to live, for 80% of sellers, by Diwali."
task:
Write a requirements list from these notes, grouped under headings:

1. **Business objective**: with a measurable target
2. **Functional requirements**: numbered (`FR-1`, `FR-2`, …), each one testable, starting with *"The system shall…"*
3. **Non-functional requirements**: numbered (`NFR-1`, …): performance, security, retention, device support
4. **Assumptions and open questions**: what you still need to confirm and with whom

Aim for 5–8 FRs and 3–5 NFRs. Don't design screens; state *what*, not *how*.
hints: The objective is already in the notes: 10 days application-to-live for 80% of sellers by Diwali. Write it so it can be measured.
Every pain point suggests a requirement: blurry photos → check image quality at upload; status calls → status notifications; GSTIN typed by hand → automatic GSTIN validation.
"Low-end Android and 3G", "keep for 8 years", "only my team can see" are non-functional: they constrain *how well* the system works, not *what* it does.
Open questions are a sign of a good BA: Which notification channel? Which GST API, and its cost? What image-quality threshold? Who approves exceptions?
explanation:
Good requirements are **specific, testable and solution-neutral**. Compare:

- ✗ *"Make document upload better."*
- ✓ *"FR-1: The system shall check each uploaded document image for readability and ask the seller to re-upload before submission if it fails."*

The second can be tested in UAT; the first can't.

Separate **functional** (what the system does) from **non-functional** (performance, security, compliance, usability) requirements, because they're tested and owned differently. Writing **assumptions and open questions** explicitly is how a BA avoids building the wrong thing; each should name who will answer it.

Also notice what's *not* a requirement: "four people in KYC" is context, and "field agents go smoother" is an insight to explore (why?), not a feature.
interview:
*"After interviewing the seller operations head, I translated her notes into a business objective with a measurable target, eight testable functional requirements and four non-functional ones covering 3G performance, access control and 8-year document retention, plus a list of open questions with owners. It became the baseline for the BRD and cut the back-and-forth with engineering in sprint planning."*

Expect: **"How do you handle conflicting requirements from two stakeholders?"** Trace each back to the business objective, make the trade-off visible, and get the sponsor to decide.

rubric: States the business objective with a measurable target and date
Functional requirements are numbered, testable and start with 'The system shall'
Covers document quality checks, bank verification, GSTIN validation and seller status updates
Non-functional requirements cover performance on low-end devices/3G, access control and 8-year retention
Requirements say what, not how (no screen designs or technology choices)
Lists assumptions or open questions, each with who will answer it
